PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Etiquette is the way we speak and act so that other people feel respected. In this sub-strand you will practise the sounds /e/, /eɪ/, /p/ and /b/, recognise polite words and phrases, and use them when you ask, thank, apologise or welcome someone.

## Strand 3.0: Etiquette
Sub-strand 3.1.1: Listening and Speaking: Pronunciation and Vocabulary
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
b) identify polite words and phrases in a conversation for communication
c) pronounce words and phrases containing target sounds accurately for effective communication
d) use appropriate words and phrases to show politeness in different contexts
e) promote the use of using polite words and phrases in different contexts

## What this sub-strand covers
• Polite words and phrases
• Target sounds

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should we pronounce sounds and words clearly?
2. Which words do we use to show politeness?

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This is developed as the learner works with peers to practise saying words and phrases containing the sounds.
• Learning to Learn: It is enhanced as the learner builds onto their learning experience by using polite words and phrases in different contexts.

## Values
• Unity: This promoted as the learner teams up with peers to recite a poem featuring polite words and phrases.
• Respect: The value is developed as the learner appreciates individual differences and accommodates diverse views when solving word puzzles.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Social Cohesion: This is developed as the learner appreciates the use of etiquette to promote harmonious co-existence and interpersonal relationships.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to link the concept of pronunciation and vocabulary to their learning in Kiswahili.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Language Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 3.0 Etiquette, Sub-strand 3.1.1 Pronunciation and Vocabulary

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: The sounds /e/, /eɪ/, /p/ and /b/

LESSON 1: THE SOUNDS /E/, /EꞮ/, /P/ AND /B/
===========================================

## What you will learn
• Hear and say /e/ and /eɪ/.
• Hear and say /p/ and /b/.
• Write target words from dictation.

Curriculum outcomes: c) pronounce words and phrases containing target sounds accurately for effective communication

## Introduction
Pen and pain share most of their sounds, yet they are different words. Pen is something you write with. Pain is the feeling when something hurts. Your ear has to catch the vowel, and your mouth has to make it.

## Notes
### /e/ as in welcome
/e/ is the short vowel in bed, pen, men, guest, help and welcome. Your mouth is slightly open and the sound is quick. You often see it spelled e (pen, men, guest).

Say: welcome, guest, help, men, ten.

### /eɪ/ as in may
/eɪ/ is a glide. It starts near /e/ and moves toward the vowel in "see". You hear it in may, say, day, they, name and plate. The polite phrase "May I" begins with this sound. Spellings include ay (may, say, day), ey (they) and a followed by a consonant and a silent e (name, plate).

Pairs to hear:
- pen /e/ and pain /eɪ/
- men /e/ and main /eɪ/
- wet /e/ and wait /eɪ/
- get /e/ and gate /eɪ/
- sell /e/ and sail /eɪ/

### /p/ and /b/
Both sounds begin with the lips pressed together. Then the lips open and air pops out.

- /p/ has no voice. Your throat is quiet: please, polite, pardon, people, cup.
- /b/ uses the voice. Your throat buzzes: borrow, beg, bed, big, bread.

Put your fingers on your throat. Say /p/, then /b/. Only /b/ buzzes.

Pairs: pen and ben, pet and bet, pack and back, cap and cab, pig and big.

Please begins with /p/. Beg, as in "I beg your pardon", begins with /b/. Borrow begins with /b/. If you swap them, the word changes.

### Tongue twisters
Say each one slowly, then a little faster. Stop if the sounds smear together, and start again slowly.

- Ben's pen is better than Pete's pen.
- Ten men met the guests and said welcome.
- May they say the name the same way.
- Please beg Ben to pass the bread.

### Dictation
When someone dictates, they say a word and you write it. Listen for the vowel and for /p/ or /b/ before you write. Helpful words: please, beg, pardon, borrow, welcome, may, pen, bed, guest, they.

Check the spelling after you have listened. Please has ea. Borrow has a double r. Welcome has one l, not two.

## Key words
• /e/ — the short vowel sound in pen, bed and welcome
• /eɪ/ — the glide in may, say and they
• /p/ — the voiceless lip sound at the start of please
• /b/ — the voiced lip sound at the start of borrow

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which word has /eɪ/: men, may or bed?

Working:
1. Men and bed have the short vowel /e/.
2. May has the glide /eɪ/.

Answer: may

### Example 2
Is the first sound in please voiced or voiceless?

Working:
1. Please begins with /p/.
2. Put a hand on your throat and say /p/.
3. The throat does not buzz.

Answer: Voiceless

## Activity: Tongue twisters and dictation
You will need: The tongue twisters in this lesson, Exercise book, A digital device only if the teacher plays a recording
1. Say the four tongue twisters with a partner, slowly and then faster.
2. Listen to words with /e/, /eɪ/, /p/ and /b/ read by the teacher or played from a device. Repeat each word.
3. Write ten of the words from dictation.
4. Swap books and check the vowel and the first consonant together.

## Practice
1. Write the /eɪ/ partner of pen, men and get.
2. Which words begin with /b/: please, borrow, beg, pardon?
3. How can you feel the difference between /p/ and /b/?
4. Write please and borrow, taking care with the vowels and the double letter.

## Summary
• /e/ is short, as in pen. /eɪ/ glides, as in may.
• /p/ is voiceless and /b/ is voiced. Both use the lips.
• Tongue twisters and dictation train the ear and the hand together.

### Answers to practice
1. pain, main, gate
2. borrow and beg
3. Put your fingers on your throat. /b/ buzzes and /p/ does not.
4. please, borrow

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Polite words and phrases

LESSON 2: POLITE WORDS AND PHRASES
==================================

## What you will learn
• Identify polite words and phrases in a conversation.
• Say what each common phrase is used for.
• Use polite phrases in sentences for real situations.

Curriculum outcomes: b) identify polite words and phrases in a conversation for communication; d) use appropriate words and phrases to show politeness in different contexts

## Introduction
"Give me that pen" and "May I borrow your pen, please?" ask for the same object. Only one of them shows courtesy. The words we choose tell people whether we respect them.

## Notes
### Words this theme uses
Etiquette means good manners. Courtesy is polite behaviour. A rude remark ignores another person's feelings. These are the phrases to learn and to hear:

- excuse me: to pass someone, to interrupt, or to get attention
- please: to make a request softer
- May I: to ask permission
- thank you: to show you are grateful
- welcome: to greet a visitor, or to reply to thanks ("You are welcome")
- I am sorry: to apologise
- I beg your pardon: to apologise, or to ask someone to repeat what you did not hear
- congratulations: to show joy for another person's good news
- borrow: to take something for a time and then give it back

### Hear them in a conversation
Neema: Excuse me, may I come in?
Teacher: Yes, welcome. Please sit down.
Neema: Thank you. I beg your pardon, I am a little late.
Teacher: That is all right.
Musa: Congratulations on your neat work, Neema.
Neema: Thank you. May I borrow a pen, please?
Musa: Yes. You are welcome.

Polite phrases in that talk: excuse me, may I, welcome, please, thank you, I beg your pardon, congratulations, borrow, you are welcome.

### Match the phrase to the moment
- You want to pass a group at the door: Excuse me, please.
- You want a book that is not yours: May I borrow your book, please?
- Someone gives you a seat: Thank you.
- You step on a friend's foot: I am sorry.
- You did not hear: I beg your pardon?
- A classmate wins a race: Congratulations.
- A visitor arrives: Welcome.

"May I" is a question, so the voice rises a little at the end, and the sentence ends with a question mark when you write it.

### A puzzle of polite words
Hide the words in a box of letters or scramble them: esalpe (please), orworb (borrow), yrros (sorry is inside "I am sorry"). Trade puzzles. Finding the word is not enough. Say the phrase it belongs to.

## Key words
• etiquette — polite behaviour, including the words we use with other people
• courtesy — polite and considerate behaviour
• permission — agreement that you may do something
• apologise — to say that you are sorry

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which phrase fits when you did not hear a question: "What?" or "I beg your pardon?"

Working:
1. What? can sound rude.
2. I beg your pardon? asks for a repeat with courtesy.

Answer: I beg your pardon?

### Example 2
Identify the polite phrases in: "Excuse me, may I borrow your ruler, please?"

Working:
1. Excuse me gets attention.
2. May I asks permission.
3. Please softens the request.
4. Borrow tells what you want to do.

Answer: Excuse me, may I, please, and the polite use of borrow.

## Activity: Polite-word puzzle
You will need: Paper, Pencils, The conversation in this lesson
1. Read the conversation aloud in pairs and underline every polite word or phrase.
2. Make a puzzle together: scramble please, borrow, sorry, welcome and pardon.
3. Another pair solves the puzzle and says a full polite sentence for each word.
4. Construct two new sentences: one asking to borrow something, and one apologising.

## Practice
1. What do you say when you want permission to come in?
2. Which phrase thanks someone, and which phrase apologises?
3. Replace the rude request with a polite one: "Give me your pencil."
4. When do we say congratulations?

## Summary
• Polite phrases include excuse me, please, may I, thank you, sorry, welcome and congratulations.
• Match the phrase to the moment.
• A request sounds courteous when it asks permission and includes please.

### Answers to practice
1. Excuse me, may I come in?
2. Thank you shows thanks. I am sorry apologises.
3. May I borrow your pencil, please?
4. When we are glad about another person's good news or success.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Using courtesy in different places

LESSON 3: USING COURTESY IN DIFFERENT PLACES
============================================

## What you will learn
• Choose polite words for home, school and a visit.
• Recite a short poem that uses those phrases.
• Explain why a community is kinder when people use them.

Curriculum outcomes: d) use appropriate words and phrases to show politeness in different contexts; e) promote the use of using polite words and phrases in different contexts

## Introduction
The same polite words travel with you. You use them with a grandparent at home, with a teacher at school, and with a visitor at the gate. The place changes. The respect does not.

## Notes
### The same courtesy, different places
At home: "Please may I have some water?" "Thank you for the meal." "I am sorry I forgot my chore."

At school: "Excuse me, may I ask a question?" "Thank you for helping me." "Congratulations on your drawing."

With a visitor: "Welcome. Please come in." "May I take your bag?" "I beg your pardon, could you say your name again?"

You do not need different manners for different people. A younger child and an older guest both deserve please and thank you.

### A poem to recite
Please and Thank You

Excuse me, may I pass this way?
Please may I borrow your pen today?
Thank you for the seat you gave.
I am sorry I was not brave
Enough to ask, but now I say,
Welcome, friend, and have a good day.
Congratulations on your prize.
I beg your pardon. I dropped your book. Let me lift it. There it lies.

The last two lines are longer so you can hear "I beg your pardon" inside a real apology. Practise them slowly so /p/ in please, pardon and prize stays crisp, and /b/ in borrow stays voiced.

### Promote the habit
To promote polite words means to use them often enough that other people catch them. You can:

- Say the phrase yourself instead of only telling others to be polite.
- Thank a classmate who says excuse me.
- Recite the poem together so the phrases stay in your mouth.
- Gently offer a better sentence when a friend sounds rude: "Try 'May I', and I will pass it to you."

Etiquette helps people live together. A class, a family and a queue are more peaceful when requests are kind and apologies are quick. You do not have to be perfect. You do have to keep choosing the courteous sentence.

### Clear sounds still matter
A mumbled "sorry" can sound like nothing. Say the phrase so the listener hears it. Look at the person, speak at a steady pace, and mean the words. Courtesy that cannot be heard does not do its work.

## Key words
• promote — to support something and help it spread
• request — the act of asking for something
• habit — something you do often, almost without being told

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You are at home and you want to leave the table. Which sentence shows courtesy?

Working:
1. A command is rude in this moment.
2. Ask permission and include please.

Answer: Excuse me, may I leave the table, please?

### Example 2
How can one learner help a rude phrase disappear without a quarrel?

Working:
1. Offer the polite form.
2. Use it yourself.
3. Thank people who use it.

Answer: Model the polite sentence, for example "May I borrow it, please?", and thank others when they use courtesy.

## Activity: Recite and use the poem
You will need: Copies of Please and Thank You
1. Team up and recite the poem until the polite phrases are easy to hear.
2. Each learner picks a place: home, school or a visit. Say two sentences you would use there.
3. The group listens for please, may I, thank you, sorry, welcome, congratulations or pardon.
4. Agree on one habit the class will promote this week, such as saying excuse me before interrupting.

## Practice
1. Write a polite sentence you could use when a visitor arrives.
2. Write a polite sentence for the classroom when you want to ask a question.
3. What does it mean to promote polite words?
4. Why should an apology be spoken clearly?

## Summary
• Use the same polite phrases at home, at school and with visitors.
• A poem keeps the phrases ready in your mouth.
• Courtesy spreads when people hear it and copy it.

### Answers to practice
1. Any correct sentence, for example: Welcome. Please come in.
2. Any correct sentence, for example: Excuse me, may I ask a question?
3. To use them often and encourage others to use them too.
4. So the other person hears it and knows you mean it.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 3.1.1 LISTENING AND SPEAKING: PRONUNCIATION AND VOCABULARY
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word has the vowel /eɪ/?
   A. pen
   B. bed
   C. may
   D. help

2. Which word begins with voiced /b/?
   A. please
   B. pardon
   C. borrow
   D. people

3. Which pair contrasts /e/ and /eɪ/?
   A. pen and pain
   B. pen and ben
   C. cap and cab
   D. boy and toy

4. Which phrase asks someone to repeat what you missed, politely?
   A. What?
   B. I beg your pardon?
   C. Give it to me
   D. Go away

5. What do you say to a friend who has just won a prize?
   A. Excuse me
   B. Congratulations
   C. I beg your pardon
   D. May I leave

6. Which sentence is polite?
   A. Give me your book.
   B. May I borrow your book, please?
   C. I take this now.
   D. Pass that.

7. You step on someone's foot. What should you say?

8. Which response welcomes a visitor?
   A. Congratulations
   B. Welcome. Please come in.
   C. I am a little late
   D. Borrow my pen

9. Why do we promote polite phrases in class?

10. Why should please and sorry be pronounced clearly?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 3.1.1 LISTENING AND SPEAKING: PRONUNCIATION AND VOCABULARY
========================================

1. C. may
   May has the glide /eɪ/. The others have short /e/.

2. C. borrow
   Borrow begins with /b/. Please, pardon and people begin with /p/.

3. A. pen and pain
   Pen has /e/ and pain has /eɪ/.

4. B. I beg your pardon?
   I beg your pardon? is the courteous request for a repeat.

5. B. Congratulations
   Congratulations shows joy for another person's success.

6. B. May I borrow your book, please?
   May I asks permission and please softens the request.

7. I am sorry.
   I am sorry is the phrase for an apology.

8. B. Welcome. Please come in.
   Welcome and please come in greet a visitor with courtesy.

9. So that people hear them, use them, and live more peacefully together.
   Etiquette spreads by example.

10. A mumbled phrase may not be heard, so the courtesy does not reach the other person.
   Clear sounds make the polite message work.

LESSON 2: POLITE WORDS AND PHRASES
==================================

## What you will learn
• Identify polite words and phrases in a conversation.
• Say what each common phrase is used for.

LESSON 3: USING COURTESY IN DIFFERENT PLACES
============================================

## What you will learn
• Choose polite words for home, school and a visit.
• Recite a short poem that uses those phrases.
• Explain why a community is kinder when people use them.

Curriculum outcomes: d) use appropriate words and phrases to show politeness in different contexts; e) promote the use of using polite words and phrases in different contexts

The same polite words travel with you. You use them with a grandparent at home, with a teacher at school, and with a visitor at the gate. The place changes. The respect does not.

## Notes
### The same courtesy, different places
At home: "Please may I have some water?" "Thank you for the meal." "I am sorry I forgot my chore."

At school: "Excuse me, may I ask a question?" "Thank you for helping me." "Congratulations on your drawing."

With a visitor: "Welcome. Please come in." "May I take your bag?" "I beg your pardon, could you say your name again?"

You do not need different manners for different people. A younger child and an older guest both deserve please and thank you.

### A poem to recite
Please and Thank You

Excuse me, may I pass this way?
Please may I borrow your pen today?
Thank you for the seat you gave.
I am sorry I was not brave
Enough to ask, but now I say,
Welcome, friend, and have a good day.
Congratulations on your prize.
I beg your pardon. I dropped your book. Let me lift it. There it lies.

The last two lines are longer so you can hear "I beg your pardon" inside a real apology. Practise them slowly so /p/ in please, pardon and prize stays crisp, and /b/ in borrow stays voiced.

### Promote the habit
To promote polite words means to use them often enough that other people catch them. You can:

- Say the phrase yourself instead of only telling others to be polite.
- Thank a classmate who says excuse me.
- Recite the poem together so the phrases stay in your mouth.
- Gently offer a better sentence when a friend sounds rude: "Try 'May I', and I will pass it to you."

Etiquette helps people live together. A class, a family and a queue are more peaceful when requests are kind and apologies are quick. You do not have to be perfect. You do have to keep choosing the courteous sentence.

### Clear sounds still matter
A mumbled "sorry" can sound like nothing. Say the phrase so the listener hears it. Look at the person, speak at a steady pace, and mean the words. Courtesy that cannot be heard does not do its work.

## Key words
• promote — to support something and help it spread
• request — the act of asking for something
• habit — something you do often, almost without being told

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You are at home and you want to leave the table. Which sentence shows courtesy?

Working:
1. A command is rude in this moment.
2. Ask permission and include please.

Answer: Excuse me, may I leave the table, please?

### Example 2
How can one learner help a rude phrase disappear without a quarrel?

Working:
1. Offer the polite form.
2. Use it yourself.
3. Thank people who use it.

Answer: Model the polite sentence, for example "May I borrow it, please?", and thank others when they use courtesy.

## Activity: Recite and use the poem
You will need: Copies of Please and Thank You
1. Team up and recite the poem until the polite phrases are easy to hear.
2. Each learner picks a place: home, school or a visit. Say two sentences you would use there.
3. The group listens for please, may I, thank you, sorry, welcome, congratulations or pardon.
4. Agree on one habit the class will promote this week, such as saying excuse me before interrupting.

## Practice
1. Write a polite sentence you could use when a visitor arrives.
2. Write a polite sentence for the classroom when you want to ask a question.
3. What does it mean to promote polite words?
4. Why should an apology be spoken clearly?

## Summary
• Use the same polite phrases at home, at school and with visitors.
• A poem keeps the phrases ready in your mouth.
• Courtesy spreads when people hear it and copy it.

### Answers to practice
1. Any correct sentence, for example: Welcome. Please come in.
2. Any correct sentence, for example: Excuse me, may I ask a question?
3. To use them often and encourage others to use them too.
4. So the other person hears it and knows you mean it.

questions.question: Which word has the vowel /eɪ/?
questions.explanation: May has the glide /eɪ/. The others have short /e/.

questions.question: Which word begins with voiced /b/?
questions.explanation: Borrow begins with /b/. Please, pardon and people begin with /p/.

questions.question: Which phrase asks someone to repeat what you missed, politely?
questions.explanation: I beg your pardon? is the courteous request for a repeat.

questions.question: What do you say to a friend who has just won a prize?
questions.explanation: Congratulations shows joy for another person's success.

questions.question: Which sentence is polite?
options: May I borrow your book, please?
questions.explanation: May I asks permission and please softens the request.

questions.question: You step on someone's foot. What should you say?
questions.explanation: I am sorry is the phrase for an apology.

questions.question: Which response welcomes a visitor?
questions.explanation: Welcome and please come in greet a visitor with courtesy.

questions.question: Why do we promote polite phrases in class?
questions.answer: So that people hear them, use them, and live more peacefully together.

questions.question: Why should please and sorry be pronounced clearly?
questions.answer: A mumbled phrase may not be heard, so the courtesy does not reach the other person.
questions.explanation: Clear sounds make the polite message work.
